claims.feature: reading standard: account for every detail
claims.claim: The critic's test for a Wolfe reading is a consistent account of why everything in the text is there, in a story of under 3,000 words.
claims.quote: why everything that's in the text is there

claims.claim: Names are always important in Wolfe stories; Stromboli evokes Pinocchio and the planet Sarg the marionettist Tony Sarg.
claims.quote: Names are always important in Wolfe stories.

claims.claim: Central plot points are skipped over and referred to only in retrospect, others presented misdirectingly, others never cleared up.
claims.quote: Central plot points are skipped over

claims.feature: liar plus translator frame leaves motive underdetermined
claims.claim: Because Severian is known to lie and Wolfe poses as translator of a manuscript for an unknown audience, the text's purpose and the narrator's motives are underdetermined.
claims.quote: underdetermined with regard to Severian's motives

claims.feature: archaic Latinate words that look like neologisms
claims.claim: The style uses words that appear to be neologisms but are archaic, often Latin-derived usages, evoking strangeness while preserving meaning.
claims.quote: words that appear to be neologisms but are anything but

claims.claim: Auerbach reports Clute's argument that the whole narrative is a put-on to justify Severian's taking power.
claims.quote: a put-on to justify Severian taking power

claims.claim: After The Book of the New Sun Wolfe abandoned baroque long sentences and strove for a more minimalistic surface text.
claims.quote: abandons the baroque and long sentences

claims.feature: subtext replaces text in late work
claims.claim: In the post-Wizard Knight novels the subtext tends to replace the text, and Wolfe plays less fair by withholding metatextual repetitions.
claims.quote: The subtext tends to replace the text.

claims.claim: Aramini's reading principle: something is true about almost every detail, literally or figuratively, so he reads without suspicion and makes everything true somehow.
claims.quote: everything has to be true somehow, literally or figuratively

claims.feature: two mysteries that explain each other
claims.claim: Wolfe sometimes plants two confusing things that explain each other, as with the context-free gunfight and the off-screen death in Home Fires.
claims.quote: the two mysteries explain each other

claims.feature: literalized metaphor and repeated unrelated fact
claims.claim: Wolfe controls meaning through logic, small details, literalized metaphors and juxtaposing unrelated things; tunnel dogs called gods signal that gods are stored in the tunnels.
Embedded tales map allegorically onto the larger story, and symbols are built to yield concrete plot conclusions.
claims.quote: embeds tales which map allegorically to the larger story

claims.claim: Wolfe told Nigel Price that, having so often been called a difficult writer, he strove in later works to make his style simpler and more accessible.
claims.source: Aramini interview, Ultan's Library 2020 (Price reporting Wolfe)
claims.quote: make his style simpler and more accessible

claims.feature: classic detective stories as stylistic model
claims.claim: Price suggests Wolfe's late reading of Rex Stout and Sayers supplied the stylistic model for his late books, e.g. Wizard Knight as heroic fantasy channelling Stout.
claims.quote: they provided the stylistic model for his writing

claims.feature: elided structures point to one solution
claims.claim: Aramini holds Wolfe is a modernist who merely pretends to inconclusive subjectivity; his elided structures point at implied correct conclusions.
claims.quote: merely pretends to create inconclusive subjectivity
